title: LP, NLP and line search
rows: 90 min review · 10 min break · 80 min new material
Calculate first; use the demo to test your prediction.

title: Today’s schedule
rows: 0–55 min: LP, duality and shadow prices
100–180 min: line search, demos and practice

title: Opening questions
rows: Do any resource prices give an upper bound on profit?
Does ∇f = 0 prove that a point is a minimum?
Does a descent direction work with every positive step size?

title: What the dual variables mean
rows: u = price per unit of resource 1
v = price per unit of resource 2
w = 4u + 5v: value of the available resources

title: Derive one dual constraint per product
Why the dual gives an upper bound
rows: For any feasible pair: z ≤ w

title: An optimality certificate
rows: Both are feasible; equal values prove optimality.

title: Complementary slackness
rows: At optimal feasible pairs: λᵢsᵢ = 0 and xⱼtⱼ = 0.

title: Check both zero products
rows: All four products vanish; z = w = 9.

title: Practice: test a proposed price
rows: Check both dual constraints and compute w.
Can w bound every feasible primal profit?

title: Solution: feasibility comes first
rows: The proposed prices are not dual feasible.

title: Derive the shadow-price interval
rows: Keep b₂ = 5 and change b₁ only.
Solve x + y = b₁ and 2x + y = 5.

title: Feasibility determines the interval
rows: x ≥ 0 requires b₁ ≤ 5; y ≥ 0 requires b₁ ≥ 2.5.
On 2.5 ≤ b₁ ≤ 5: primal z = b₁ + 5 = dual w.
At the endpoints, use one-sided slopes.

title: Inside the interval: b₁ = 4.2
rows: The shadow-price prediction is exact here.

title: Why producing y gives the larger profit
rows: For b₁ = 6: y ≤ 5 − 2x for every feasible plan.

title: Shadow prices are slopes of the value function
rows: Use the slope only within its valid segment.

title: Demo 1: change resource capacity
rows: Predict the optimum at b₁ = 2, 4.2 and 6.
Move the slider; compare actual profit with the old-price prediction.
Watch which resource has unused capacity.

title: LP checkpoint
rows: At b₁=6, write the unused amount of each resource.
Find feasible dual prices whose value equals 10.
Does an active constraint always have a positive price?

title: Convexity requires a domain-wide check
rows: Assume f is C² on an open convex domain.
Convex ⇔ Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere.
A Hessian check at one point is not enough.

title: A stationary point may be a maximum
Check values and classify the point
rows: Thus x = ±1 are global minima; x = 0 is a local maximum.

title: One gradient step is not the optimum
rows: Let rₖ = (uₖ,vₖ). Use α = 0.1: r₁ = r₀ − α∇f(r₀).

title: Practice: compute the second step
rows: Compute the new gradient, point, and objective.
Does reusing the old gradient give the same method?

title: Solution: update the gradient every time
Derive the constant-step convergence range
rows: Let eᵤ = u−1 and eᵥ = v+2.
Both shrink for every start when 0 < α < 0.25.

title: Newton directions also need a check
NLP checkpoint
rows: For q(x)=(x²−1)², classify x=0 and x=±1.
For the quadratic, explain why α=0.25 can fail if kept fixed.
Before line search, what sign should gᵀp have?

title: Break · 10 minutes
rows: Keep the quadratic and the starting point in your notes.
Next: choose a step size automatically.

title: Direction and step size
rows: αₖ is the step size (textbooks: step length); distance moved = αₖ‖pₖ‖.

title: Check the direction first
rows: With g = ∇f(r), require gᵀp < 0 for descent.
This guarantees decrease for sufficiently small positive α.

title: A one-dimensional function along the ray
Exact line search for this quadratic
A large step can increase the objective
Armijo sufficient decrease
rows: Accept α if f(r+αp) ≤ f(r) + c₁αgᵀp.
The accepted value must beat a target below f(r).

title: Backtracking parameters
rows: If Armijo fails, replace α by ρα and test again.

title: Acceptance depends on c₁
rows: With c₁=0.0001, α=0.25 passes the first search.
Its target is 19.9932, and the actual value is 17.
One accepted step does not justify keeping that α forever.

title: The two loops
rows: Outer loop: compute g and choose a descent direction p.
Inner loop: keep r,p fixed; test α, ρα, ρ²α, …
After acceptance: update r, then recompute g.

title: Demo 2: inspect each Armijo trial
rows: Accept the step, then inspect the NEW gradient.

title: Practice: one-dimensional backtracking
rows: Minimize f(x)=3x². Start at x=1, so p=−6.
Find the first accepted α and the new point.

title: Practice solution
rows: New point x=−0.5: f drops from 3 to 0.75, but x* = 0.

title: Compare complete runs
rows: Use the same start (3,0) for every method.
Fixed α=0.1 converges; fixed α=0.25 stalls above 0.
Backtracking (c₁=0.1) reaches (1,−2) in two steps; exact arrival is special to this example.

title: Python demonstration
rows: Run line_search_lab.py or open the notebook.
Print α, actual value, target and accept/reject.
Change the start or c₁, then explain the new trace.

title: Stopping and reporting
rows: Check ‖g‖, objective, iteration count and finite values.
A tiny step or small change can mean stagnation.
For nonconvex problems, also inspect curvature and multiple starts.

title: Line search cannot repair every direction
rows: For q at x=0.2: Newton gives p≈−0.21818 and gp>0.
Small positive steps in this direction increase q.
Replace the direction, for example with p=−g, before descent search.

title: BFGS: a preview
rows: Newton solves Hp=−g using the Hessian.
BFGS updates a curvature approximation using changes in r and g.

title: Exit check
rows: Why was α=0.25 rejected when c₁=0.1?
What stays fixed during the inner backtracking loop?
What must be checked before a descent line search?

title: Exit check: answers
rows: 17 > 13.2: the decrease is insufficient for this target.
Keep the current point r and direction p fixed.
Check gᵀp < 0. If g = 0, stop and classify the point.
